scores.evidence: Put on-prem database in **read-only**; app queues writes ... Promote cloud database to primary; switch app, load balancer and DNS
scores.rationale: Mechanisms (CDC, read-only freeze, promote, reverse replication) are correct; minor issues like 15-second lag check and DMS reverse replication feasibility and DNS caching are glossed.

scores.evidence: Writes pause for under 60 seconds at cutover, during the quietest hour.
scores.rationale: Sensibly redefines no downtime, covers core needs, and is buildable; the plan leaves gaps on vendor licensing and app queuing feasibility (noted as an assumption).

scores.evidence: Set up the interface engine so it can send to either environment, controlled by a configuration switch.
scores.rationale: Consistent single-writer design with clear phases; minor loose ends such as who owns write queueing and the 'reads never stop' claim while on-prem is read-only.

scores.evidence: Rehearse the full cutover and rollback at least twice in a staging environment, and time each step.
scores.rationale: Reconciliation, load at 1.5x peak, failover tests, and rehearsals target main risks, but criteria like rollback thresholds are unquantified and there is little post-launch validation beyond hypercare.

scores.evidence: The plan assumes the system is a standalone app (vendor-built or in-house) with its own database, connected to the EHR through HL7.
scores.rationale: Assumptions and sensitivity questions are explicit; some figures like 60s and 1.5x are unjustified, and effects are only briefly explained.

scores.evidence: Rollback triggers: errors above threshold, HL7 messages backing up, data mismatch, or response time worse than baseline.
scores.rationale: Covers double-booking, hidden integrations, and rollback, but lacks handling of duplicate or lost HL7 messages, replication divergence, queued-write failures, and adversarial inputs.

scores.evidence: Hypercare (2–4 weeks): IT staff on site at scheduling centers, dashboards for errors, response time, and HL7 queue depth.
scores.rationale: Hypercare, dashboards and a command center are present, but ongoing monitoring, incident ownership, access admin and schema or deployment practices are thin.

scores.evidence: Consider keeping on-prem as a warm standby for the first 30–90 days.
scores.rationale: Cost is essentially not discussed beyond the dual-running period; no drivers, estimates or controls.

scores.evidence: Rehost or lightly replatform first ... Leave redesigning the application for after the move; don't change the code and the location at the same time.
scores.rationale: Avoids re-architecture and keeps rollback, but the lock-in, data model and identifier choices and exit paths are little discussed.

scores.evidence: True zero write-pause needs two-way replication with conflict handling. I don't recommend it for scheduling
scores.rationale: Picks the simpler one-way sync with a brief write freeze; components are justified, though some optional items such as a pilot clinic and the WAF add minor overhead.

scores.evidence: | T-0 | Put on-prem database in **read-only**; app queues writes |
scores.rationale: Phased timeline and a timed runbook give concrete sequencing and checkpoints, though tool choices and go/no-go thresholds are left open.

checklist.evidence: Business Associate Agreement (BAA) signed with the cloud provider. Use only services covered by it.
Interface engine | Rhapsody, Cloverleaf, Mirth, etc.: all endpoints, IP/firewall rules, hard-coded hostnames
Reconcile data every day: appointment counts per day, provider, and location, plus checksums on key tables.
Writes go to one database only; brief write freeze
Start reverse replication cloud → on-prem, which keeps rollback possible
dedicated private link (AWS Direct Connect or Azure ExpressRoute) ... with a site-to-site VPN as backup. Test latency from every clinic site.
set target recovery times and data-loss limits. Consider keeping on-prem as a warm standby
Identity | Active Directory/LDAP, SSO, service accounts
Load tests: at least 1.5× historical peak.
Hypercare (2–4 weeks): IT staff on site at scheduling centers
Wipe disks securely, with certificates of destruction.

traps.evidence: Load an initial database copy, then turn on continuous change replication from on-prem to the cloud.
Two databases taking bookings at once can cause double-booked slots
no public database endpoints, a web application firewall in front of the patient portal
Integrations are where hospital migrations usually fail, so map all of them
don't change the code and the location at the same time.

note: A sound single-writer, replicate-then-switch plan with a rehearsed rollback and a good integration inventory. It is weak on cost, break-glass access, clinical downtime procedures, the shadow validation of interface messages, and ongoing operations.
